Hey there! Game designer and tech enthusiast here, and I'll actually go into the nitty-gritty as to why gamepads just aren't built for First Person Shooter/pointer-based games.

Please take note that I have no ill opinion of either mouse or gamepad input devices, and that I merely staunchly believe that different inputs are designed for specifically different ways of play (it is why, for example, FPS titles are "more at home" on the PC with a keyboard and mouse than on the console where they're forced to adopt half measures to make up for the inherent inaccuracies of thumbstick-based inputs, such as the aforementioned aim assist that PC FPS's don't have to worry about).

 

Thumbsticks, functionally, for aiming in an FPS environment is inferior to a mouse - a peripheral created to be the pointing device. They are designed specifically to permit input of constant motion (which is counter-intuitive for the needs of a pointing device that requires incremental motion), with a mechanically built-in unavoidable deadzone inherited by its design (where the transitioning point between "looking to the right" and "looking to the left" is interrupted by a zone where there's no motion or input that can be detected by the input device, and a biologically-based limitation where your wrist muscles are used for the majority of the needed precision to accurately interface with the game by proxy of the input device - in this case, the thumbstick. On top of all of this, the speed at which you can aim is restricted by both software and hardware, as there's a maximum angle at which the thumbstick can be tipped.

A mouse, conversely, is an input device that doesn't have constant motion, and thus has no "deadzone" of input where movement is not registered (save for a default resting, non-moving state), which earned its place on the desktop with PC's. Because it's on a surface, the entirety of the arm can be used from a comfortable resting position (which is where the Wiimote fails, along with its cheap components - but that's for another story) which utilises everything from your upper body to all 5 of your digits to influence its movement (particularly in a claw grip), and the speed at which it can be moved is not as limited by the hardware of the device (even while true, you can have a limit in place for mouse sensitivity). You can physically move the mouse as fast as you can - which is why players can pirouette on the spot with ease in PC FPS's. Snapping between two positions can be an instant for a mouse, whereas there's a built-in travel time for the thumbstick brethren.

 

As such I believe that consoles should either adopt a nunchuck (where the thumbstick allows for movement, not aiming)+mouse setup, or, FPS games should just not be developed for consoles as in order to make them function, training wheels in the form of aim assist and bullet magnetism are required. These mechanisms to counter the inherent inaccuracies of thumbsticks water down and make the skill gap smaller, and as a result negatively affect the game's quality from its gameplay to how its ranking system operates.

tl;dr: thumbsticks aren't made to be a pointing device, they never were, and the competitive quality of FPS games suffer from trying to use them as input devices as they're forced to make do with the limitations of the hardware, mechanically and biologically, by implementing aim assist to make up for that fact, which ultimately ends up narrowing the skill gap, negatively influencing ranking systems as a result.

And even if you did make a console shooter with no aim assist/etc, the differences in what players are capable of across platforms (god save you if it's a multi-platform game that's also available for the PC) would be so dramatically huge that headshots would look like they happen once-in-a-blue-moon with thumbsticks when compared to a PC that has a keyboard and mouse. It's not so much that using a mouse is necessarily easier but that being forced to use thumbsticks is pointlessly overly difficult due to the previously mentioned limitations.
